article_text:
H aving something as terrible as a ghost appear to a child was regarded by Henry James as one turn of the screw - to two children, two turns. M Night Shyamalan confirmed the first half of that in The Sixth Sense, and now Alejandro Amenabar completes the axiom with his sturdily old-fashioned and tremendously enjoyable ghost story, set in occupied Jersey in 1945.

As in his previous two films, the Chilean-born Amenabar has written, directed and even composed the musical score - how many auteurs can say as much? This is his first English-language film and one of the scariest things about it is just how fluent Amenabar is in period English. This is a 29-year-old born in Santiago; he has lived mostly in Spain, yet he dashes off lines such as “Cowardy cowardy custard!” like a master. Has he had secret coaching from Anthony Buckeridge or JK Rowling? (Amenabar says he loved Agatha Christie and Enid Blyton as a child - enough to read them in the original, I guess.)

His leading lady is Nicole Kidman , as Grace, the Catholic mistress of a gaunt old country seat, denuded of most of its traditional household staff, though not its heavy furniture and oppressive atmosphere. She is waiting for her husband to return from the war - a conflict for which he volunteered. This abandonment is the source of much unstated grief and reproach.

Alone, Kidman manages their two young children with a natural patrician severity. It is a manner she transfers, only slightly modified, to addressing the staff: three sinister characters who arrive at the beginning of the film to replace servants who have (mysteriously) fled: Fionnula Flanagan as the housekeeper-cum-nanny, Elaine Cassidy as the mute skivvy, and, of all people, Eric Sykes, playing it dead-straight as the gardener.

All of them must be instructed in the strange eternal darkness in which they live: the children’s photosensitive condition means they must always be locked indoors, exposed to nothing stronger than candlelight. The newcomers’ arrival coincides with uncanny happenings and noises: the trembling of a chandelier, the sound of Chopin coming from the empty music room with its locked grand piano - and then Grace’s daughter Anne calmly, in fact rather crossly, announcing that she is being bothered at night by a small ghostly boy called Victor who sometimes teases, sometimes cries uncontrollably.

Kidman gives a very beautiful, statuesque performance as Grace, exquisitely turned out by designer Sonia Grande in a sumptuous pastiche of 1940s English tailoring: a thousand times better cut and better designed than anything she could have got hold of at the time. There is one scene in which, roused in panic from her bed, Kidman displays some very spiffy silk pyjamas and an elegant, loosely tied dressing gown. Perhaps only she, among the A-list leading ladies, has the height to carry off this ensemble.

Her glacial stare, furious, afraid – or both – is the most pointed thing about this performance, sometimes deployed so that those glassy eyes each contain a tiny reflection of the flickering lamp that she has pulled up to her face in the dark. It is either addressed straight to the camera, or sometimes in profile, so that we can see Kidman’s distinctive, even characterful nose: a little too prominent to be snub. This is the sexiest she has ever been, by far.

But it is Kidman’s relationship with the children which is the real joy of the film. Anne and Nicholas, played by Alakina Mann and James Bentley, are excellent in a pert and unselfconsciously knowing way that I haven’t seen since the heyday of BBC teatime drama. Nicholas is cowering, placid, demanding on his mama’s attentions and affections; Anne is clever, mature, contemptuous of the silliness of children and grownups. Mann and Bentley have a charm wholly absent from the humourless, self-important demeanour of Haley Joel Osment. With Kidman they have some terrific scenes in which they quarrel over Bible stories and the instructions that Anne gets in preparation for her first holy communion – cleverly combining humour with a miasma of guilt and fear of judgment and the afterlife.

The cinematography by Javier Aguirresarobe doesn’t stray far from classic generic boundaries: the fast, swooping shot up a gloomy corridor, accompanied by Amenabar’s pleasingly trad shuddering violins, the shocking, disorientating encounter with the face in the mirror, then turning to the distraught original - all these moves are brought off in with great style and confidence, and he has a coolly heart-stopping scene in which a glowering face in the dark turns out to be the portrait of some distant civil war ancestor. Managed with less skill, it might have been absurd; here it delivers an effectively nasty jab.

What a relief to have a scary movie instead of a Scary Movie - no boring irony, no tiresome inverted commas. It is well constructed, as opposed to incompetently deconstructed. Whether or not you are actually scared depends on a willing susceptibility. But providing that submission is accomplished - well, many is the pleasurable and invigorating frisson to be had.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "今年的釜山双年展汇聚了多位艺术家，共同构建出集体性的声音表达，以此作为铭记历史、挑战既有体制以及构想另类未来的工具。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2026年釜山双年展在港口城市举行，汇聚了来自22个国家的46位艺术家及艺术团队，主题为“异见合唱团”（Dissident Chorus）。展览由伊芙琳·西蒙斯（Evelyn Simons）与阿马尔·哈拉夫（Amal Khalaf）共同策展，将声音置于材料与表达形式的前沿，同时聚焦身体如何成为档案馆以及抵抗的工具。", "links": [{"text": "Evelyn Simons and "双年展启用了3个场地，其中包括位于乙淑岛（Eulsukdo Island）的釜山现代美术馆，该岛是一座生态公园兼候鸟栖息地。这一地点自然延续至展览的第一部分，探讨再生与地理，以及代际与生态关切。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "约书亚·塞拉芬（Joshua Teeradakorn）同样将物品用作信息共享的工具，通过消费品以及T恤、钥匙扣和别针等旅游纪念品来实现这一目的。《记忆阈值：混沌共振》（Memory Threshold: Chaos Resonance，2026）还包含一个植根于政治主题的声音装置，艺术家借此质疑重复与生产在传播信息中的角色，并探讨哪些叙事被淡化或变得更迎合文化消费。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "柳成实（Sungsil Ryu）宏大的《万梦图》（TEN THOUSAND "text": "原釜山南高等学校位于影岛（Yeongdo Island），该校于今年早些时候刚刚腾空，如今成为双年展的又一展区。阿里亚斯卡尔·阿巴卡斯（Aliaskar Abarkas）的作品《咒语》（Spell，2026）位于室外运动场上，是一件通过集体运动进行学习的参与式作品。回收纺织品采用几何图案和保护符号进行安装，随着每一步的迈出，在土地上勾勒出一个音乐乐谱。", {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这所学校也成为了一个进行反思去学、质疑叙事和重构观念的场所。在一个废弃的教室背景中循环播放着录像，课桌上点缀着合成头发、蕾丝以及饰有织物套和绘画的玉米片包装盒，这是法蒂玛·哈利姆·خان（Fatima Khaleem Khan）的作品《泼出去的牛奶》（Spilt Milk，2026）中的场景。这些麦片来自一个巴基斯坦军方背景的企业集团，该集团还资助国家支持的电视台并运营学校课程。这件作品探讨了谁在控制知识、知识是如何被消费的，以及知识的传播方式如何通过家庭、学校和电视塑造身份认同和行为。在另一间教室里，詹灿霍罗尔·额尔德尼巴亚尔（Jantsankhorol Erdenebayar）的作品《本土的共振》（Resonance of the Vernacular，2026）深入探讨了集体记忆、蒙古文化、劳动力，以及人们如何适应政治、环境和经济变化。由木材、绳索、金属和人造皮毛等各种材料制成的椅子，暗示了游牧传统以及与自然世界不断变化的关系。正对着教室的是一块贴满镜子碎片和突出的角的黑板，这里是体制系统成为过去、现在、共同抱负与个人价值观之间意识形态紧张冲突的场所。", "translated": true}, {"type": ETERNO》。2023。单通道录像、声音、彩色。10分钟27秒。图片由艺术家与Mendes Wood DM画廊提供。前景：于连·克鲁泽（Julien Creuzet）。《Zumbi Zumbi Eterno, out in the open, far off near the horizon, we blinked, hoping to see the green gleams, on the line of orange ash that fears sea salt, we hallucinated, the tide, the bitter remorse, far from the foreign land》，2026。综合媒介。尺寸不固定。釜山双年展组委会委任创作，2026。Ⓒ 釜山双年展组委会。保留所有权利", "credit": "Canvas", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "同样位于影岛的另一个双年展场地是 Space OneZ，这是一座改造自百年历史的船用仓库，外面停泊着货轮。该地点捕捉了釜山的港口及其海洋历史，这些历史由跨越水域分享的关于劳作、生存、暴力以及人类与非人类神话的故事所塑造。于连·克鲁泽（Julien Creuzet）的《ZUMBI ZUMBI ETERNO》（2023）占据了第一个空间的大部分，成为一件纪念碑式的装置作品。祖比（Zumbi）指的是巴西逃亡奴隶聚落（quilombola）领袖，也被称为帕尔马雷斯领袖祖比（Zumbi Dos "text": "布拉希姆·塔尔（Brahim Tall）的《不和谐唱诗：海洋的创造》（2025）置于仓库的另一个开口处，将19个扬声器围成一圈，它们都在低语。每个音频都放置在提供声音者的身高位置。他们各自作为个体发声，但合在一起则成为一种超越自身的、凝聚一体的共享声音。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在整个釜山，本届双年展凝聚为对声音的探索，它超越了言语和旋律，概括了运动、记忆、历史、知识、创伤与治愈。通过装置、电影、声音、雕塑和参与式作品，艺术家们对何谓发声、记忆和抵抗做出了不同的诠释。每个人演唱不同的声部，但他们共同体现了一种统一的号召：正视过去，寻找理解、归属感，或许还有一次重塑世界当前轨迹并重新想象新的生活与思考方式的机会。", "translated": true}, article_text:
This year’s Busan Biennale brings together artists to form collective sonic expressions that serve as a tool for remembering the past, challenging systems and imagining alternative futures.

Taking place in the port city, the 2026 Busan Biennale has brought together 46 artists and teams from 22 countries under the theme of Dissident Chorus. Curated by Evelyn Simons and Amal Khalaf , the exhibition foregrounds sound as a material and form of expression while focusing also on how the body becomes an archive and tool for resistance.

The biennale activates three sites, including the Busan Museum of Contemporary Art on Eulsukdo Island, an ecological park and habitat for migratory birds. The location carries through into the first part of the exhibition with themes of regeneration and geography, as well as generational and ecological concerns.

Joshua Serafin’s installation creates a spiral corridor structure leading to a three-channel film installation entitled Whispering Pleas of the Eternal Echoes (2026). In a fragmented exploration of ancestry and migration, the videos navigate family histories across generations and countries as they shape identity, resilience and belonging while proposing a new universe where all connections merge.

Similarly defying linear boundaries, Yazan Khalili’s interactive installation We carry our pain like a language (2026) presents 39 hats embroidered with a section of poetry, with each hat available to purchase by the public. As the caps are bought, worn and disappear, the poem disperses and becomes impossible to understand in its entirety. Only through collecting knowledge of all of the parts does its message reach through the crowd and beyond, avoiding censorship or institutional barriers. Tanat Teeradakorn also utilises items as a tool for sharing information, through consumables, tourist souvenirs such as t-shirts, keychains and pins. Memory Threshold: Chaos Resonance (2026) also includes a sound installation grounded in political themes as the artist questions the role of repetition and production in circulating messages and in questioning what narratives become diluted or more palatable for cultural consumption.

Sungsil Ryu’s monumental TEN THOUSAND DREAMS (2026) presents scissor-lift platforms hosting zombie-like uniformed children in varying states of decay, accompanied by three musical tracks. The work combines children’s voices with hopeful melodies exhorting one to dream big and achieve one’s goals, with an underlying eerie critique on societal pressures and capitalism that questions how human ambition was shaped and consumed as an alternative to South Korea’s lack of natural resources.

The location of the Former Busan Nam High School on Yeongdo Island was only vacated earlier this year, and is now another site for the biennale. Aliaskar Abarkas’s Spell (2026) is situated outside on the sports field, as a participatory work to learn through collective movement. Reclaimed textiles are installed using geometric patterns and protective symbols to create a musical score traced into the land with each step.

The school also becomes a place for unlearning, questioning narratives and reframing notions. A looping video plays in the background of an abandoned classroom and desks are dotted with synthetic hair, lace and cornflake boxes with fabric covers and drawings in Fatima Khaleem Khan’s Spilt Milk (2026). The cereal is from a Pakistani military-linked conglomerate that also funds state-backed television and operates school curricula. The work probes who controls knowledge, how it is consumed and the way in which its transmission shapes identity and behaviour through home, school and television. In another classroom, Jantsankhorol Erdenebayar’s Resonance of the Vernacular (2026) delves into collective memories, Mongolian culture, labour and how people adapt to political, environmental and economic change. Chairs made from various materials­ – such as wood, rope, metal and faux fur – allude to nomadic traditions and changing relationships to the natural world. Facing the classroom is a chalk board collaged with mirror fragments and protruding horns as a site where institutional systems are sites of ideological tension between past, present, shared ambitions and personal values.

Also in Yeongdo is the other biennale location, Space OneZ, a converted century-old marine warehouse, with cargo ships docked outside. The location captures Busan’s port and its marine history, shaped by stories shared across waters of labour, survival, violence and human and non-human myths. Julien Creuzet’s ZUMBI ZUMBI ETERNO (2023) inhabits the majority of the first space as a monumental installation. Zumbi references the Brazilian quilombola leader, also known as Zumbi Dos Palmares, who resisted Portuguese colonial rule At the centre of the work is a film where jellyfish and toxic puffer fish drift by and symbols of life, death and transformation converge. Surrounding the video are several cars wrapped in textiles, almost as relics left to succumb to their surroundings. The piece becomes an exploration of the ocean as a space of memory and as a living archive, connecting the past of suffering and resistance with industry and cultural identity as the human and non-human become intertwined.

Placed at the other opening of the warehouse is Brahim Tall’s The Choir of Dissonance: The Creation of the Sea (2025), which places 19 speakers in a circle, all whispering. Each audio is positioned at the height of each person who shared their voice. They each speak as individuals, but together become a shared sound uniting to form something beyond themselves.

Across Busan, the biennale comes together as an exploration of sound that becomes more than words and melodies to encapsulates movement, memories, history, knowledge, trauma and healing. Through installations, film, sound, sculpture and participatory works, the artists create different interpretations of what it means to speak, remember and resist. Each sings different parts, but collectively they embody a unified call to acknowledge the past and search for understanding, belonging and perhaps a chance to redirect the current trajectory of the world and reimagine new ways of living and thinking.

Busan Biennale 2026 runs until 1 November

article_text:
It’s double trouble.

AMC Theatres has released the first look at its new “ Dune: Part Three ” collectible popcorn buckets. And to send Paul Atreides off in style, the theatre chain has not one, but two designs, including one bucket that has two sandworm heads. The other, a “Sandworm Thumper” bucket, boasts a “working Thumper design.” For those not versed in all things spice, the Thumpers are what Fremen warriors place in the desert sands to summon the worms from their subterranean homes.

The designs are, how shall we put it, a little NSFW. Their resemblance to popular sex toys was parodied in a SNL sketch in which a frisky adolescent’s thoughts turned to something other than popcorn when he looked at the sandworm’s gaping mouth.

The company said that the double sandworm bucket is perfect for couples, because it’s “easier to share popcorn.” There’s also a light-up cup, though no word on pricing. Buckets typically cost in the neighborhood of $25. “Dune: Part Three” opens December 18, 2026, and brings back franchise stars Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya, and Rebecca Ferguson, as well as director Denis Villeneuve.

The collectibles have become big business for the chain, with AMC chief Adam Aron projecting the company will make more than $100 million selling the themed buckets this year.

AMC has released collectible buckets timed to major films such as “The Devil Wears Prada 2” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” but the chain acknowledged that all eyes were on them for their “Dune” follow-up.

“The AMC Sandworm popcorn bucket for ‘Dune: Part Two’ became a viral phenomenon, and we knew that ‘Dune’ fans would have high expectations for what came next,” said Hank Green, AMC’s senior VP of food and beverage. “From the moment we started planning the ‘Dune: Part Three’ collectibles, our goal was to exceed those fan expectations. The Sandworm Thumper and Double Sandworm collectibles take the experience to the next level with designs straight from the movie.”

In other words, cue the memes.

article_text:
L’Espagne de mon enf(r)ance*

She knew her grandmother, who lived in a neighbourhood where Spanish exiles had recreated their own little Spain. She felt immersed in that atmosphere. However, people spoke to her in French. She was there, and they were somewhere else. As a quiet child, people used to tell her: ‘Well then, have you lost your tongue ?’ She never learnt to speak Spanish. She first sought to fill these silences by meeting Spanish exiles in France, then by travelling the length and breadth of Aragon, the land her grandparents had left before their exile. But she could not find her place; the two territories, the two timeframes, remained divided. A turning point led her to her family’s archive photographs; she felt the need to plunge into the gap. It was by intervening on the very fabric of her images that she was able to reinterpret the world in which she grew up. She tore, erased, scraped, then re-glued, assembled, superimposed and transported to Spain these hybrid, hand-crafted photographic objects. She saw the void transform into flesh. This living material has brought depth to the anonymous part of her history. Removed from its intimate context, this work speaks to a collective memory, questions the effects of exile on subsequent generations and creates the framework for a transformation of the past into the present.

* (The title cannot be translated because the word enf(r)ance is a contraction of enfance (childhood) and France).

article_text:
The Directors Guild of America’s Women’s Steering Committee has announced its seventh class of mentors and mentees. The mentorship program pairs mid-career women and nonbinary directors with established mentors to help them navigate the early days of their careers.

Lucia Aniello (“Hacks,” “Broad City”), Mike Flanagan (“Carrie,” upcoming “The Exorcist: Martyrs”), Boots Riley (“I Love Boosters,” “Sorry to Bother You”), Karyn Kusama (“Jennifer’s Body,” “Girlfight”) and former DGA president Lesli Linka Glatter (“Mad Men,” “Homeland”) are among this year’s cohort of mentors.

“It is our mission to cultivate and strengthen the careers of our SQUAD cohort,” said directors and program co-leaders Karla Braun, Jess Brunetto, Tiffany Frances and Alexis Ostrander in a joint statement. “We believe these incredibly talented directors deserve every opportunity to reach the next level and beyond.”

“Amid the ongoing contraction of our industry, the WSC and DGA’s commitment to building this community is more meaningful than ever,” the statement continues. “Together, we are creating a space where we can support, champion and empower one another. We are inspired by these mid-career directors and cannot wait to see what they accomplish next.”

The WSC Squad Mentorship Program, which first began in 2021 , is a nine-month curriculum aimed at cultivating a collaborative community of directors equipped with the tools and knowledge that will lead members toward success, while also having discussions about the challenges that women directors face in the process.

In addition to Braun, Brunetto, Frances and Ostrander, the WSC is co-chaired by directors Shaz Bennett, Jade Jenise-Dixon, Valerie Weiss and alt co-chair Liz Ryan.

The seventh class of mentor-mentee pairs are Lucia Aniello and Carmen Angelica; Abe Sylvia and Shaz Bennett; Kat Candler and Sabrina Doyle; Shannon Murphy and Claire Fowler; Gandja Monteiro and Saray Guidetti; Mike Flanagan and Anna Halberg; Boots Riley and Tiffany Johnson; Geeta V. Patel and Manjari Makijani; Karyn Kusama and Kate Sullivan; Jake Schreier and Alissa Torvinen; Lesli Linka Glatter and Mallory Thompson; and Laura Belsey and Kristin Windell.

article_text:
Academy CEO Bill Kramer is set to make his first trip to Japan later this month. He will collect a leadership award at the Tokyo International Film Festival and also sit down with Toho president and CEO Matsuoka Hiro for a public conversation.

The festival’s 39th edition runs Oct. 26–Nov. 4 and has built a program titled Academy in Tokyo around the visit. Two colleagues will join Kramer in the Japanese capital: Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor and Meredith Shea, the organization’s chief membership, impact and industry officer.

Related Stories

Jennifer Lopez to Release New Single ‘Proof of Love’: ‘It's a Happy Dance Song’ That Also Addresses ‘Pain and Grief When Someone’s Gone’ (EXCLUSIVE)

The three executives will share a stage on Oct. 28 at Tokyo Midtown Hibiya Hall for a 90-minute panel moderated by TIFF festival director Hisamatsu Takeo. They will take the audience behind the curtain of the Oscars and outline the Academy’s international initiatives and membership programs. The conversation will also turn to how the organization views international cinema today and where it is heading.

Once the panel wraps, Kramer will receive TIFF’s Global Cinema Leadership Special Award. The festival said the honor recognizes his contribution to the growth of the worldwide film business and to film culture. Later that day, the Academy will hold a private reception for its members from across the globe.

Other senior Academy figures will also be in Tokyo for the festival and the member reception. Among them are Amy Homma, who oversees the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and the Academy Collection as director and president; Jenny Galante, the Academy’s chief revenue and business development officer; and Jennifer Davidson, its chief marketing, communications and content officer.

Kramer returns to the same venue on Oct. 29 to sit down with Matsuoka. Their session will look at the state of the global film landscape and the outlook for theatrical and streaming distribution, along with ways to deepen cross-border partnerships. Both public events are free, though advance reservations are required. Booking details have yet to be released.

Kramer took the Academy’s top job in 2022. Before that, he ran the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures as its director and president. The museum opened its doors in September 2021. As CEO, Kramer has pushed to broaden the Academy’s 11,000-strong membership and give it a more international makeup. He runs the organization’s global operations, from the Oscars and the Academy Foundation to the $500 million Academy100 campaign.

Howell Taylor is in her second term as president. She is an Oscar-nominated producer whose credits include “A Star Is Born,” “The Accountant,” “Captain Fantastic” and “Blue Valentine.” She joined the Academy’s Producers Branch in 2014. She also co-produced the 92nd Oscars telecast in 2020, which earned her an Emmy nomination.

Shea is the first person to hold her post. Her remit covers membership, awards administration and talent development. It also includes the Academy’s outreach to film festivals and international territories.

Matsuoka has steered Toho’s expansion overseas, including its acquisitions of Gkids and Anime Limited. He also oversaw the production of Oscar winner “Godzilla Minus One.” In 2025, Toho posted its best-ever results at the Japanese box office. Matsuoka also sits on the board of trustees of the Academy Museum.

TIFFCOM, the content market that runs alongside the festival, takes place Oct. 28–30.

Source: Atsushi Nishijima

Yorgos Lanthimos’s ‘Poor Things’ filmed on soundstages in Budapest

The Hungarian film industry is abuzz with what is being described as a “cultural reawakening”, as a new government ushers in a plethora of fresh appointees and stabilises a crucial financial incentive for producers.

Led by new prime minister Peter Magyar, who took office in May, the government has appointed producer Viktoria Petranyi of Proton Cinema as ministerial commissioner with a brief to oversee the renewal of the Hungarian film support system. The wider aim is to bring back transparency and democracy to public life after what many regarded as the authoritarian excesses of the Viktor Orban era, when the right-wing, populist Fidesz party was in power for 16 years.

“There are burning issues in the film industry, and even more pressing problems in film culture,” says Petranyi.

Over the summer, Ervin Nagy, Hungary’s state secretary for culture, dismissed the entire directorial board of the National Film Institute (NFI) state body as well as its commissioner Csaba Kael. By July, a controversial cap placed on the 30% tax rebate for productions – a move introduced in 2025 that spooked international producers, studios and streamers, who have long flocked to Budapest to make films and series such as Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy, Brady Corbet’s The Brutalist , Yorgos Lanthimos’s Poor Things and thriller series The Day Of The Jackal – was removed.

Source: Proton Cinema

Viktoria Petranyi

“We trust the industry will soon be booming again. The tax rebate system is back on track,” insists Petranyi.

Leading producers will not specify which projects were lost because of the cap but Gabor Sipos, whose Laokoon Filmgroup produced 2016 Oscar winner Son Of Saul , confirms his company missed out on two features due to issues with the tax rebate, one from the US and one from Europe. Other local producers faced similar setbacks.

On the cultural side, Petranyi is looking to establish a new leadership of NFI.

“We want to completely isolate it from politics, rebuild the application system, analyse and integrate the film communities’ feedback into the new structure. It is essential to build trust,” says Petranyi. “The ultimate goal is to create a multi-tiered funding system and reintegrate Hungarian film into the international stream.”

There will no longer be a film commissioner leading NFI, a reflection of the wariness about “relying on a single individual to dictate outcomes”, she adds. A new director, whose appointment is due to be announced this month, will be politically independent and chosen by a jury whose members include two representatives from the film community.

Loss of trust

Many Hungarian producers have had their own trust in their national funding system shaken over recent years. During the latter part of the Orban era, many say they were cut off from support through NFI which, several claim, backed films as much on the basis of their ideological content as their artistic merit.

A generation of young filmmakers have not been able to make their debut films because of the public film policy, claim these producers, suggesting that NFI funding (which was $18m last year for fiction features including production funding, development and marketing, and will be considerably less this year) was reserved for a small circle of producers. Others were still able to use the 30% tax rebate but rarely received direct public support either through NFI or broadcasters.

Historical nationalistic epics such as Janos Szikora’s 2023 film Hadik , produced by Endre Nagy, were heavily supported by NFI while many more contemporary dramas were overlooked. Ousted commissioner Kael – who assumed the role in 2019 in the wake of Andy Vajna’s death – fiercely defends his record, telling Screen the NFI application process was fully transparent.

“The demand for state film funding we have received applications for is much higher than the allocated amount of state support,” he says. “Those who did not receive support usually sought and thought to discover political reasons – both on the right and on the left.”

During his tenure as commissioner, he points out, more than 90 films were supported by NFI and many were selected for cate­gory-A festivals. They also attracted local viewers. In the Kael era, the market share of Hungarian films rose to more than 10% while inward investment through studios and streamers increased until the slowdown caused by the rebate cap. (In 2023 alone, Hungary attracted more than $1bn in international film industry spending.) There was also heavy investment in new facilities and infrastructure.

However, both established producers and newcomers confirm they felt frozen out. “Over the past four to six years, securing film funding has required political loyalty to the system,” insists Sipos, who is also leader of the Hungarian Producers Alliance, which recently compiled its own 125-page white paper with proposals for reforming the industry. “That does not mean every producer who received financing was aligned. The National Film Institute was occasionally – but rarely – attentive to funding projects outside of that circle.”

“I have produced all my films and have built a company without national funding, which is extremely hard,” says producer Patricia D’Intino of Good Kids Productions, which she co-founded with Leo Pinter in 2017 to focus on young talent and first and second features.

Even a strongly established company such as Petranyi’s own Proton Cinema, which has produced numerous award-winning films from directors including Gabor Reisz and Kornel Mundruczo, was “really affected” by the shift in funding strategy at NFI, she confirms. According to Petranyi’s colleague, producer Julia Berkes, Proton received support for only a couple of minority co-productions during Kael’s leadership of NFI.

To keep their companies going, independent Hungarian producers have turned to shorts, documentaries and low-budget features, with many relying on service work to cover overheads. Producers acknowledge there may now be a stampede for public funding as producers apply en masse to NFI. Money is tight and many are bound to be disappointed.

“A lot of great directors have been parked; they’ve been waiting. We have so many projects piled up,” says one source.

Positive response

Source: Bernadette Mayer

Genoveva Petrovits

Filmmakers, however, are encouraged by the change in mood and approach at NFI. “They have been responding, they have been curious,” says D’Intino, who received support to attend Venice with Horizons short film Test Track by Lydia Cornett.

“We are expecting more strategic thinking and a more open-minded funding body – a funding body that will be for the independent producers,” says Genoveva Petrovits of Kino Alfa, the company behind Oliver Rudolf’s upcoming feature My Mother, The Monster .

“This generation of producers of which I am a part is very resilient,” she adds. “We figured out how to function in the previous era and I am looking forward to working with a system that is actually supporting its filmmakers.”

“After six years of not getting financed, I am not worried about anything anymore,” agrees Berkes of the newfound optimism among Hungary’s independent producers. “Compared to nothing, at least there is now a hope for something.”

Petranyi is striking a pragmatic note and is careful not to promise too much. “No money will be enough to fill the gap of the last years, so the goal cannot be to make up for lost time,” she says. “The goal is simply to create a next-level support system, with no political bias, purely based on the standards of our culture and the international market.”

Under its new director, NFI will support a broader range of films and provide opportunities for voices from marginalised communities. “Diversity, like independence, must be a fundamental baseline,” says Petranyi. “The primary way to guarantee it is by keeping politics far away from decisions, ensuring that voices can be born freely. All stories have to be told. Applications must be evaluated exclusively on professional merit.”

Tom DeSimone, who transitioned from directing adult films into helming a host of B-movies including cult pic “Reform School Girls” and talking-vagina comedy “ Chatterbox ,” died Oct. 17 in Cathedral City, Calif. He was 87.

His brother Bob confirmed his death and said he chose to die with medically assisted end of death after a terminal cancer diagnosis.

Born in Revere, Massachusetts and raised in Newton and Weston, DeSimone earned a master’s in film at UCLA and directed the low-budget 1968 adventure film “Terror in the Jungle.”

DeSimone directed numerous adult films including “Lust in the Afternoon,” “Gay Guide to Hawaii” and “Prison Girls,” often under the pseudonyms including Lancer Brooks.

In 1977, his career went somewhat more mainstream with the comedy “Chatterbox,” about a woman who discovers her vagina can talk. “Tom DeSimone’s ‘Chatterbox’ which stars the game Candice Rialson as Penny, a beautician who discovers that her vagina can talk and that it isn’t always tactful. A genuinely funny comedy, ‘Chatterbox’ is about a vagina that spouts the most politically incorrect things at the most inopportune times, much to the chagrin of the dubious assortment of men who want to bed Penny,” wrote the film blog The Passionate Moviegoer .

He went on to direct “Hell Night” and “Savage Streets,” both starring Linda Blair . DeSimone left “Savage Streets” early, moving on to direct “Angel III: The Final Chapter.” After helming “Concrete Jungle” with Jill St. John and Tracey E. Bregman, his campy 1986 “Reform School Girls” became a cult classic of the women behind bars genre, and later in the 1980s he directed four episodes of “Freddy’s Nightmares.”

His other TV directing gigs included “Swamp Thing,” “Super Force,” “Dark Justice,” “The Big Easy” and all the episodes of soap opera “Acapulco Bay.”

He is survived by his brother, Bob, sister-in-law, Lisa DeSimone, nieces Amanda and Gianna DeSimone, and grandnephew Ori DeSimone.

article_text:
Tribeca-winning helmer Darko Lungulov , behind Serbia’s Oscar candidate “ Here and There ,” and Lithuania’s Ernestas Jankauskas (“Troll Farm,” “I Am Fine, Thanks,” “Sasha Was Here”) are among a handful of seasoned filmmakers set to pitch their works in progress at Tallinn’s Baltic Event industry showcase Nov. 19, next to a swathe of exciting new voices. Those take in Bafta-nominated Welsh helmer Josh Trigg, Naomi Kawase’s protégé, coming to Tallinn with the Japanese language “Leopard Spots,” and Basque newcomer Marina Palacio with “And Thus It Will Go On” produced by Gariza Films (“Sisters,” “20,000 Species of Bees”). Meanwhile Lithuanian talent to watch and American Film Institute graduate Saulius Baradinskas, Golden Lion candidate in Venice for his short “Techno Mama,” will pitch his feature debut “Concrete Music,” a crime drama and musical set in 1990s post-Soviet Lithuania. Split across the Baltic Event Works in Progress, International Works in Progress and Just Film Works in Progress for kids and youth, this year’s rich works in progress lineup takes in 16 projects in production or post-production, selected from more than 100 submissions from all around the world. “The final selection is a great blend of different genres from psychological dramas to dark comedies and satiric self-reflections,” said works in progress co-managers Kärt Väinola and Helen Räim, who received a slew of entries from Southeast, Central Europe, Latin America and Spain. One Basque project “And So It Will Go On,” made it into the International Works in Progress, a nice addition said the co-honchos as the Basque region is spotlighted at Tallinn’s Black Nights Film Festival. Turning on overarching themes, Väinola and Räim said “the theme of family and especially the bond between parent and child runs through the whole selection, as a source of both fear and freedom.”

Related Stories

Netflix Is Profitable and Still Growing. Why Did It Just Make a Huge Round of Layoffs and Oust Its Top Content Exec?

Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE)

They also pointed at mortality and loss, “treated with rare lightness in several films,” notably in the dark comedies “A Midnight Pilgrimage,” “Marry Then Die,” “Burlaks” and “The Elderly Store,” or in the drama with fantasy elements “The Reef.” “Time and memory also appear as important central subjects in “And So It Will Go On,” and “Luci Looped in Limbo,” they observed.

Popular on Variety

For the first time, all 16 works in progress will be pitched the same day — Thursday Nov. 19 — in the morning and early afternoon to leave the filmmakers more time to discuss, mingle and create new partnerships before the Baltic Event closing ceremony Nov. 20.

Full rundown of the works in progress:

International Works in Progress

“And Thus It Will Go On” (“Y así seguirán las cosas,” Marina Palacio , Spain)

Directorial debut of rising talent Palacio, produced by high-profile Basque outfit Gariza Films (“20,000 Species of Bees,” “Sisters”). Won “most promising project” at Tallinn-Baltic Event Script Pool 2022. Hybrid pic shot over several years in which a child, Germán, lives isolate in a village, surrounded by adults and elderly people. Once reunited with his old friends in the endless fields, play becomes his way of discovering and understanding life. “Marina’s cinematic vision and storytelling skills, makes this movie a coming of age full of magic, truly hypnotic,” says exec producer Ana Angulo Umaran.

“Leopard Spots” (Josh Trigg, Japan, U.K.)

Sophomore pic from Welsh helmer Trigg, after his breakthrough film, the Bafta-nominated “Satu-Year of the Rabbit.” Produced by On Par Productions, Kingyo Films, Geronimo Boy Film. Following “Satu-Year of the Rabbit”’s top accolade at the Nara Int’l Film Festival, prominent Japanese helmer Naomi Kawase and Nara founder invited Trigg to direct “Leopard Spots” in Japan. Shot in 16mm in a small factory town in Nara, the pic “combines British social-realist sensibility with contemplative Japanese cinema,” says Toby Cameron who produces with Aiko Flores Yoshioka, Ruth Yoshie Linton. The story turns on single mother Lilly who grapples to keep her daughter close in a bitter-sweet tale of failed redemption.

“Luci Looped in Limbo” (Théo Gottlieb, France)

Feature debut of rising talent Gottlieb, starring Luzja Richter (“Phantom Thread,” “Vikings: Valhalla”) Bella Kim (“Winter in Sokcho”) and seasoned actor Pascal Grégory (“One Fine Morning,” “La vie en rose”).

Produced by Yoel Servadio for Hiersoir Films, in co-production with 84 Films. Luci, a physicist obsessed with changing the past, must learn to accept the present.

This is a pic “rooted in a deeply personal story that explores universal themes of love, loss and acceptance, with the ambition of resonating with a broad international audience,” says Servadio. “Bringing together a French and Korean cast in a multilingual narrative, it blends science fiction with an intimate love story unfolding across a lifetime. Rather than using time travel and sci-fi as a spectacle, the film explores our desire to hold on to what inevitably changes, combining a high-concept premise with emotional depth and a distinctive multicultural identity.”

“Požari” (“Fires,” Nina Tratnik, Montenegro, Albania, Serbia)

Debut feature. As wildfires close in on Podgorica, Ana (18) has to take care of her dying grandmother, secretly recording her parents on her phone, and uncovering the desires and long-buried tensions tearing her family apart. Produced by Code Blue production with Era Film, Cinnamon-CinneRent, Radio & Television Montenegro.

“Without You” (“Uden Dig,” Nil Holst-Jensen, Denmark)

Psychological thriller from the director of the TV series “Where Were You.” Produced by Daniel Mühlendorph for Hyæne Film. Sine feels trapped by motherhood due to her demanding daughter, Ida. When Ida suddenly disappears, Sine’s world is shattered, yet her lost freedom, old friends, and acting career unexpectedly return. Everything she ever wanted comes within reach, as long as Ida doesn’t return.

“The Elderly Store,” (Karylar dukonu,” Amanbek Azhymat, Kyrgyzstan)

Sophomore feature by Azhymat whose debut “Backstage Madness” screened at PÖFF in 2025. Absurd and darkly humorous drama, offering an unconventional take on aging, loneliness and human dignity. “At the center of the film is a paradoxical world in which an elderly person must prove his usefulness in order to earn the right to continue living,” says associate producer Elvira Mamytova.

Baltic Event Works in Progress

“A Midnight Pilgrimage” (“Öised rännakud,” Katrin Ruus, Estonia)

Poetic tragicomedy from newcomer Ruus, written by Estonia’s prominent filmmaker Peeter Urbla, recipient of a PÖFF Lifetime Achievement in 2022. Urbla and Sander Lebreht produce for Exitfilm. When tragedy strikes, a carefree journalist must step up to anchor his family and rebuild his world. Toplining the cast are Indrek Sammul and Kristina Preimann. “Katrin Ruus looks at a man’s grief with patience and tenderness, and lets the audience stay with him long enough to understand him. At a time when everyone is asking where men fit in, this film doesn’t lecture. It listens,” says Lebrecht.

“Marry Then Die” (“Apprecēties un mirt”, Elza Gauja, Latvia)

Gauja who won best film at the Latvian Film Awards 2024 for “Postcard from Rome,” comes back with a dark romantic tragedy built around an unusual pact. Zigis, a charming drifter, will help Anya, a suicidal widow, to end her life, but only if they marry first! Produced by one of Latvia’s most established outfits VFS Films . “Elza Gauja’s distinctive directorial style-warm, playful and deeply attentive to human contradictions-allows difficult subjects to coexist naturally with humour and tenderness,” says Līva Vernere who produces with Uldis Cekulis. Pitched at the 2024 B.E. Co-Production Market.

“Concrete Music” (“Betono muzika,” Saulius Baradinskas, Lithuania, Italy)

Feature debut from one of Lithuania’s most exciting new voices, American Film Institute graduate Baradinskas, who’s short “Techno Mama” bowed in Venice. Crime drama and musical set in 1990s post-Soviet Lithuania starring Domantas Starkauskas. Musically gifted teenager Rokas, runs away from his mafia family to use music as a way to take revenge on his father, responsible for his mother’s death. Italy’s Andrea Gori (Lumen Films) co-produces; the music is composed by Andrea Boccadoro. “Burlaks,” (“Burlaki,” Gatis Ungurs, Latvia, Georgia)

Mythological modern comedy by debut helmer Ungurs about flawed hero Miervalds, a sawmill worker who, disgusted by his boring life, embarks on a journey to a mythical mountain village where he becomes a wager between God and the Devil. Kristele Pudane -Cannes Latvian Producer on the Move 2025- produces with Dace Siatkovska for Sunday Rebel Films, in co-production with Georgia’s Half Alien Films.

“Paraiso, Outer Space,” (Carlos E. Lesmes, Estonia)

Experimental and personal film by Colombia-born Estonia-based Lesmes whose doc “A Loss of Something Ever Felt,” premiered at Hot Docs 2020. “A walk in the Bardo illuminated by city lights, a sea of connections that look like people,” reads the logline. Produced by the helmer and Lili Pilt for Tin Can and Hare Films. Just Film Works in Progress

“Uncle Egg,” (“Onkel Egg,” Torfinn Iversen, Norway, Germany)

Sophomore pic by Norwegian writer/director Iversen, Crystal Bear nominated in 2017 with “Oskar’s America.”“Game of Thrones’ Kristofer Hivju stars as the titular character, the eccentric Uncle Egg, who travels to Germany with his nephew Hauk (12) from Northern Norway, to help him find his biological father. Martin Müller The search turns into quite a challenge as 25,000 men in Germany carry the same name. Produced by Fjordic film.

“The Queen of England Stole My Parents” (“Anglijos karalienė pagrobė mano tėvus,” Ernestas Jankauskas, Lithuania)

From one of Lithuania’s leading production and serving outlets Dansu Film, co-producer of Netflix’s “Clark” and producer of Lithuania’s first high-quality TV show “Troll Farm” helmed by Jankauskas. Feature spinoff of the helmer’s short film of the same name, which bagged best short at the Lithuanian Film Awards 2014. Deeply personal film about adoption co-penned by producer Gaibja Siurbyte -Jankauskas’ partner. Smiltė (10), an adopted girl embarks on a journey to save her biological parents from the Queen of England.

“The film follows a girl in foster care through a magical, often absurd adventure. It’s funny, but it doesn’t look away from what she’s going through,” says Viktorija Rimkutė who produces with Siurbyte. The script is co-penned by Aleksandra Chmielewska.

“The Reef” (“Strandgut,” Phillip Donnellon, Germany, Estonia, Finland)

From the director of the Palme d’or short film nominated “Bird in the Wire.”

Adapted by Jytte-Merle Böhrnsen from the novel ”Karikko” by Seita Vuorela. Produced by Eyrie Entertainment, in co-production with Stellar Film Tack Films, and Gretchenfilm, in association with Split Second Films Limited. Little Dream Pictures handles German distribution, Yle Finnish TV rights and Epsilon Film world sales.

Producer Daniel Ehrenber says the pic uniquely “brings together two things that don’t often go hand in hand in films for young audiences: the excitement of a gripping adventure and an honest exploration of grief and loss. Inspired by the imaginative tradition of stories like “Peter Pan” and “The Brothers Lionheart,” it takes young audiences on a journey that is thrilling, mysterious and full of wonder, while gradually revealing a deeply emotional story at its heart.”

“1970,” (Darko Lungulov, Serbia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Croatia)

From the acclaimed director of “Here and There” (Best N.Y. Narrative at Tribeca), Karlovy Vary-selected “ Monument to Michael Jackson .”

Set in 1970 Yugoslavia, it follows Draško (13), who, abandoned by his parents, runs away with Erzika (16). Drifting from place to place, swept into anti–Vietnam War protests during Nixon’s visit, free love, wild rock concerts, and decadent parties, his journey home becomes an awakening to heartbreak, loss, and freedom. “Although set more than 50 years ago, it is very much a story about today as it takes us back to a time when young people believed in the possibility of changing the world,” said the helmer, who was inspired by his own childhood memories. “Set against the backdrop of Yugoslavia’s counterculture movement, this intimate coming-of-age story speaks to a new generation struggling to find its voice and its place in a world that often seems to offer little hope.” Produced by Lungulov and Snezana van Houwelingen for This and That Productions with Papa Films (Serbia), Mirage Film (Hungary), Samsa Film (Luxembourg), PomPom Film (Croatia).

“All Girls,” (Всички момичета,” Boyana Avdjieva, Bulgaria)

Social drama from actor-turn director Avdjieva who stars in it. Produced by On Pointe Productions. Avdjieva describes her pic as a “raw, distinctly female portrayal of adolescent friendship, the intensity of girlhood and the heartbreak of bonds that fall apart, set against the social realities of 2000s post-socialist Bulgaria as the country steps into the EU.” “Inspired by the events of the 2001 “Indigo” club tragedy in Sofia and similar recent cases in Europe, this independently made Bulgarian debut brings together exclusively young talent to tell a story of a generation’s fragile hope for a better future and the cost of continuing to believe in it,” she adds.

Archives – October 16, 2019

If you ask me to sum up in one word my feelings about Nathaniel Goldberg’s photography, the word “d é licatesse ” comes first. Subtle, radiant, peaceful: the images created by Goldberg through twenty-five years of a rich and productive career allow us to see a world in which the attention to the beauty of the things goes with a sensitive respect for it. Nathaniel Goldberg is a man one could call a “great soul”. Logically, his work testifies of a true humanism, particularly rare and precious in an art world often marked by the egocentrism of many artists. Goldberg knows how to watch, and through his photographs, we as a viewer, also learn how watch and indeed how to see – surely the highest achievements of a visual art. In those images, the photographer isn’t controlling his models but dialoguing with them; never he aims to directly capture a subject or a personality directly, but lightly approaches the spirit of the things his eye observes. Portrait, fashion, landscape, documentary: composed with images selected and edited by the photographer himself, this book is definitely what we call an “artist book”. Displaying various themes and heterogeneous subjects like waves of memories, this panoramic summary of Goldberg’s photographic work looks in a sense like a self-portrait. In this portraits, model Stella Tennant appears perhaps as the heart of the photographer’s work. Aristocratic and punk, feminine and masculine, Stella embodies the delicate balance of the contraries the art of Goldberg searching out. Both fascinating and disturbing, India is naturally a land of paradoxes Nathaniel Goldberg will explores: “One needs three lives to know India”, a proverb says. article_text:
At Kunsthaus Bregenz in Austria, American artist Torkwase Dyson transforms architecture into an exploration of Black geographies, environmental justice and the politics of spatial freedom.

Who has the freedom to occupy, shape and move through space? In her first solo exhibition in Austria, Torkwase Dyson challenges the notion of geography as neutral, examining how histories of slavery, colonialism and capitalism continue to influence our environments.

Presented at Kunsthaus Bregenz, the exhibition brings together monumental sculpture, painting, animation and sound, transforming the museum’s architecture into an immersive investigation of movement, boundaries and belonging.

On the ground floor, two enormous black sculptural forms, which Dyson calls hypershapes, interrupt the building’s open interior. Rooted in her theory of Black Compositional Thought, these structures explore how Black communities have historically imagined and created spaces of autonomy.

Elsewhere, a darkened gallery combines stop-motion animation, sound and paintings, while large-scale abstract compositions reference waterways and infrastructures shaped by colonial histories.

Created specifically for the museum, the works extend Dyson’s ongoing investigation into the relationship between bodies, built environments and systems of power.

The exhibition invites audiences to experience architecture not simply as a physical structure, but as a contested space shaped by history, identity and human possibility.

This exhibition is on view at Kunsthaus Bregenz in Austria, until 24 January 2027.

article_text:
Kim Jackson is a long-time independent film producer at Evotion and is behind films like “Blue Caprice,” “King Cobra,” and “Trust Machine: The Story of Blockchain.” She also serves as president of the Board of New York Women in Film & Television.

When I read the first draft of “The Plea,” a creative swirl turned into a strange synchronicity of events and positioning of people. Partially inspired by what was happening in Alabama, it felt like a movie was inevitable. I’ve watched the dismantling of Roe v. Wade, and it infuriated me.

There was an interesting story developing in Alabama. Embryos at an IVF clinic had been destroyed. Whether it was accidental or on purpose wasn’t the point. The owners of the embryos wanted justice. These women wanted some recourse over the loss of their reproductive plans. Who is responsible for the murder of their future children?

When I discovered what was going on in Alabama, I had already made the decision to quit producing movies. Movies were supposed to have the power to change the world. I wasn’t so sure anymore. It no longer brought me joy, and I was getting tired of fighting for exhibition and distribution. I’d been producing independent films for a long time. I started at a studio, but that kind of life wasn’t for me. That kind of corporate structure and hierarchy isn’t for me. I was young and wanted the freedom to express myself as a filmmaker. Anything and everything was possible then. You need that kind of delusion in a healthy measure to make indie films that the industry is not asking for.

More than twenty years and twenty films later, some have made money, have distribution and been acclaimed. Most have not.

You have to really love movies to be an indie producer. We have no union representation. No insurance. No pension plans. No benefits. Cast and crew can retire with some semblance of security. Producers are on their own. It is an unsung and mostly unheralded position at the indie level.

The producer is also left holding the bag when everyone else has moved on. Years later, there’s still work to be done managing a film’s intellectual property rights and corporate vehicles. And then there’s the matter of distribution. Always distribution. Every part of the filmmaking process seems to have eager participants and collaborators until you get to the distribution phase. Yes, there are many ways to engineer greater probability for success when it comes to distribution, but it only comes down to one thing and one thing only, there is much greater supply than there is demand. Basic economics and market dynamics.

The incident in Alabama kicked off in 2020. By 2024, a lower court initially dismissed the civil case and stated that embryos count as property, not people. Interesting… when does that property turn into a person? The Alabama Supreme Court disagreed with the lower court. The justices stated that a 1872 Wrongful Death of a Minor Act applied to all unborn children, regardless of whether they are inside or outside the uterus. Embryos have the same rights as children. Fascinating. This was the moment when the swirl of a movie started forming around me.

I was surprised this wasn’t bigger news across mainstream media. The ruling had created legal and criminal liability risks for fertility doctors. Multiple IVF clinics in Alabama temporarily paused their services and treatments. The debate regarding fetal personhood and access to fertility care was beginning. And what was fascinating was that women and couples, both pro-life and pro-choice, were being affected.

It also created the beginnings of a criminal legal structure around embryos. How far could the courts take this? If a woman had several embryos in an IVF clinic, could the state force her to carry all of them to term? And what about the sperm donor? What say do they have?

“The Plea,” inspired by this case and written by Zach LeBeau, Dean Imperial, and Scott Organ, hit my desk. Twelve months later, we were in pre-production. Its themes of an ever-divided America, society’s addiction to technology and personhood were timely, and it had to be made now.

It takes so much time, energy and money to make a film. You can spend one hundred million dollars, or you can spend one million dollars, either one can bring an audience to catharsis. As a journeywoman producer, my forte has been toward the lower million-dollar end of the spectrum. The path is specific and unique in this budget range. The upside is greater. The control is greater. Investors tend to be OK with only a percentage of investment returned in the form of a tax credit and deductions and losses claimed on tax returns. Making money is a bonus. A hit movie is a bonus. It’s about the art and message, or it’s supposed to be.

Every film festival cycle, there are panels and speeches about the ever-changing industry, how it’s broken and how it could be fixed. You can’t just make a film anymore without planning from the very beginning how it will be experienced by audiences. Is it commercial or art house? Is it intended for the big screen? Is it straight to streaming? Are you supposed to watch it on your phone? You need to be aware of the type of film you’re making, who the audience is and how you will reach them.

In the case of “The Plea,” we made a stylized black and white film to be experienced in the cinema with other people. Streaming just won’t do. We will refuse a distribution deal that results in no theatrical, no minimum guarantee, and no marketing dollars. I can’t waste my energy having told this story just to have it disappear into the blackhole of the streamerverse. And it’s an opportune time for our film, as microcinemas and art house cinema consortiums are on the rise.

We have control over very little in this chaotic, ever accelerating, ever expanding world. What we do have control over is precious. It’s an interesting dance for a producer to exercise control of a production. What to exert force and will over, and what to let take its natural course. It’s the same in life. A movie, just like life, is a series of decisions and the effects and consequences of those decisions. As I get older, and time becomes more important to me, I get more real with myself. I’m probably never going to stop making films. If I’m inspired, it becomes an uncontrollable, irresistible compulsion. But something needs to change. Do I need to change?

“The Plea” became one of those ideas that made all the broken things about the industry I had been fixated on less of a concern. It shifted the focus back to where it belonged, how to tell this story in the best possible way that reaches into the hearts and minds of the most people possible, in the event it does make it out into the world. It forced me to evolve my understanding of filmmaking. It doesn’t matter if movies have the power to change the world. I don’t know if they truly can. But what I do know is that movies have the power to change my world.

“The Plea” will world premiere at the 2026 Woodstock Film Festival on Friday, October 16 .

article_text:
At the Katonah Museum of Art in New York, Sonja John’s ‘Balikbayan’ explores Caribbean and Filipino heritage, immigrant resourcefulness and the relationship between cultural memory and the natural environment.

How do we construct a sense of home across different geographies and generations? In ‘Balikbayan’, artist Sonja John explores the intersections of migration, family history and cultural identity through a site-specific installation at the Katonah Museum of Art.

Drawing on her experiences in New York City and her family’s connections to Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, and the Philippines, John examines how personal memories and inherited histories shape our understanding of place. Combining collage, stencils and light, her work brings architectural structures into dialogue with botanical forms, questioning how representations of the Caribbean are constructed through memory, history and family archives.

Presented in the museum’s Pollack Family Learning Centre, ‘Balikbayan’ celebrates the ingenuity of immigrant communities and how cultural knowledge travels across borders. The installation also considers the relationship between migration, agricultural practices and environmental change, revealing how landscapes carry traces of displacement and belonging.

Visitors are invited to engage directly with the exhibition through mixed-media activities and a collaborative light installation, extending John’s exploration of creativity and cultural exchange. Through these encounters, ‘Balikbayan’ encourages audiences to reconsider home as an evolving relationship between memory, environment and identity.

This exhibition is on view at the Katonah Museum of Art in New York until 24 January 2027.

article_text:
Screen Brasil , the leading initiative from Embratur and Projeto Paradiso designed to boost the international distribution of Brazilian features, has selected two standout Brazilian films as their next recipients: Allan Deberton’s “ Gugu’s World ” and Grace Passô’s “ Our Secret .” The selection was announced today at a panel held during the Industry Days of the São Paulo International Film Festival.

Both films premiered at the Berlinale earlier in the year and have gone on to have successful festival runs, with the former becoming Brazil’s entry for Best International Feature at the 2027 Academy Awards and the latter winning the prestigious Kikito Award for Best Film at the lauded Gramado Film Festival.

“Gugu’s World” will receive support for its release in Spain, with international sales handled by Germany-based M-Appeal. “Our Secret,” the feature directorial debut of acclaimed Brazilian actor and playwright Passô (who could also be seen this year in Gabriel Martins’ “On Behalf of Our Son” and Ricardo Alves Jr.’s “The French Teacher”), will be supported for distribution in the U.S. and Canada, with Italy-based The Open Reel handling international sales.

Each film will receive $15,000 to support its international rollout, covering expenses such as subtitling, marketing, publicity and other audience-building initiatives in the selected territories.

First announced during last year’s Rio Film Festival, Screen Brasil aims to strengthen the global circulation of Brazilian cinema while showcasing the country’s cultural diversity and creative industries to international audiences. The initiative is a fortunate meeting between two organizations aligned in promoting Brazilian culture: Embratur, Brazil’s tourism agency, and Projeto Paradiso, a philanthropic organization dedicated to boosting the careers of Brazilian audiovisual talent on national and global stages. The partnership also forms part of Embratur’s broader strategy to promote Brazil internationally through tourism, culture and the creative economy.

In May of this year, Screen Brasil announced the recipients of its inaugural edition: “Papaya”, directed by Priscilla Kellen, with international sales handled by Best Friend Forever; “The Blue Trail”, directed by Gabriel Mascaro, with international sales handled by Lucky Number; and “The Nature of Invisible Things”, directed by Rafaela Camelo, with international sales handled by The Open Reel.

“Supporting the international distribution of Brazilian cinema turns feature films into key showcases for promoting Brazil’s soft power,” said Christiano Braga, Embratur’s audiovisual and creative economy coordinator. “On screens worldwide, these productions introduce foreign audiences to our rich biomes, culinary scene, and cultural heritage. This approach captures the interest of international travelers, drives the creation of specialized travel itineraries, and positions the country as a welcoming hub for film and TV productions, boosting local economies through screen tourism.”

Projeto Paradiso’s program director Rachel do Valle added that “international recognition at festivals is an important first step, but ensuring that Brazilian films reach audiences beyond the festival circuit remains a major challenge.”

“Through Screen Brasil, we want to help bridge that gap, supporting distributors and sales agents in bringing Brazilian stories to new markets and building a more sustainable international presence for our cinema,” she emphasized.

Following this selection, Screen Brasil will open a second round of applications for its expanded sophomore edition in the first half of 2027, a strategic calendar positioning that will allow the program to align more closely with the timing of international sales negotiations and festival markets. Full guidelines and application details for the next round can be found on the initiative’s official website .

Film Review

Faith and Its Contradictions in “9 Temples to Heaven”

Director Sompot Chidgasornpongse, who has a knack for patient observation, follows a single family on a quest to find a miracle.

9 Temples to Heaven (2026), dir. Sompot Chidgasornpongse (all images courtesy Playtime)

Whether scrolling past AI-generated “paintings” of Donald Trump as Jesus or videos of a mosque inside a shopping mall , the spiritual and holy coexist with the profane and commercial today. But decoding the meaning of our lives remains as alluring and difficult as it ever was. Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s 9 Temples to Heaven (2026), which recently screened at the New York Film Festival , takes a thoughtful approach to exploring the ways we choose to navigate these contradictions.

The film follows a family in Thailand, led by the middle-aged Sakol (Surachai Ningsanond), as they visit and build “merit” at nine Buddhist temples by making material offerings and prayers, in hopes of extending the life of his elderly mother, Sakuay, also referred to as “Grandma” (Amara Ramnarong). The trip is sparked by a premonition from Sakol’s employer — who has a history with prescient visions — that requires him to finish this auspicious number of visits within a single day in order to maximize blessings.

The film is Chidgasornpongse’s debut feature narrative but highlights a knack for patient observation: He previously directed the documentary Railway Sleepers and has assistant directed with Apichatpong Weerasethakul . With its long takes and wide angles that often linger on the dichotomous architecture in and around Bangkok, 9 Temples to Heaven appears to matter-of-factly catalog how Buddhism functions in Thailand amid capitalism, patriarchy, and other mundane aspects of daily life. This stillness does not necessarily imply neutrality, though.

The film opens with a small, golden altar illuminated by candles in a dark room. As more lights flicker on, we see that the altar is part of a larger golden structure with radiant statues inside a temple. Outside, workers set up chairs and a speaker practices pronouncing Sakuay’s name. They’re preparing for a funeral.
